headerTitle: MCD401 — Camera Basics, Principles and Practices
subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: History of Photography and the Camera

subjective.question: What is photography?
subjective.answer: Photography is the science, art, application and practice of creating durable images by recording light or other electromagnetic radiation, either electronically by means of an image sensor, or chemically by means of a light-sensitive material such as photographic film.

subjective.question: What is a pinhole camera?
subjective.answer: A pinhole camera is a simple camera without a lens but with a tiny aperture, a pinhole — effectively a light-proof box with a small hole in one side. Light from a scene passes through the aperture and projects an inverted image on the opposite side of the box.

subjective.question: What is a digital camera?
subjective.answer: A digital camera is a camera that captures photographs in digital memory. Most cameras produced today are digital, and digital cameras are incorporated into many devices ranging from mobile devices (mobile phones) to vehicles. Digital cameras use an electronic image sensor to create images. Unlike a film camera, the digital camera does not use photographic film.

subjective.question: What is a DSLR camera? What are its main parts?
subjective.answer: A digital single-lens reflex camera (also called a digital SLR or DSLR) is a digital camera that combines the optics and the mechanisms of a single-lens reflex camera with a digital imaging sensor. The reflex design scheme is the primary difference between a DSLR and other digital cameras. In the reflex design, light travels through the lens and then to a mirror that alternates to send the image to either the viewfinder or the image sensor. A DSLR consists of: (1) a camera lens, (2) a reflex mirror, (3) a shutter, (4) an image sensor, (5) a matte focusing screen, (6) a condenser lens, (7) a pentaprism/pentamirror, and (8) an eyepiece/viewfinder.

subjective.question: What is a camera shutter?
subjective.answer: In photography, a shutter is a device that allows light to pass for a determined period, exposing photographic film or a photosensitive digital sensor to light in order to capture a permanent image of a scene. A shutter can also be used to allow pulses of light to pass outwards, as seen in a movie projector or a signal lamp.

subjective.question: What is shutter speed? How is it measured?
subjective.answer: In photography, shutter speed or exposure time is the length of time when the film or digital sensor inside the camera is exposed to light, also when a camera's shutter is open when taking a photograph. The amount of light that reaches the film or image sensor is proportional to the exposure time. Shutter speed is measured in fractions of a second: for example, 1/250 means one two-hundred-and-fiftieth of a second. Written as 1/250, or officially as 1/250 s, this equals 4 milliseconds.

subjective.question: What is aperture?
subjective.answer: In optics, an aperture is a hole or an opening through which light travels. More specifically, the aperture and focal length of an optical system determine the cone angle of a bundle of rays that come to a focus in the image plane. In photography, the aperture is the size of the opening in the lens when a picture is taken; together with shutter speed and film speed, it is one of the pillars of photography.

subjective.question: What is aspect ratio?
subjective.answer: Aspect ratio describes the ratio between the width and height of an image, a screen, a graphic, or any similar flat element.

subjective.question: Differentiate between macro, micro and close-up photography.
subjective.answer: In general terms, the main difference between macro, micro and close-up photography is the level of magnification or reproduction ratio. When a photographer uses a conventional lens to focus in tight on a subject, it is considered close-up photography. If the subject is captured at a reproduction ratio of at least 1:1, it is considered macro photography. If the subject is captured at a reproduction ratio of higher than 1:1, it is considered micro photography.

subjective.topic: History of Photography and the Camera
subjective.question: Write a note on the history of photography.
subjective.answer: The history of photography has roots in remote antiquity with the discovery of two critical principles: that of the camera obscura image projection and the observation that some substances are visibly altered by exposure to light. Joseph Nicéphore Niépce successfully attempted to capture the image in a camera obscura with bitumen; the oldest photograph was taken in 1826. His associate Louis Daguerre went on to develop the daguerreotype process, the first publicly announced and commercially viable photographic process. The daguerreotype required only minutes of exposure in the camera and produced clear, finely detailed results. The details were introduced as a gift to the world in 1839, a date generally accepted as the birth year of practical photography. In 1841 William Henry Fox Talbot further refined the negative-to-positive process. The process of taking pictures was later refined with the transition from heavy glass plates to light, gelatin-coated flexible film.

subjective.topic: History of Photography and the Camera
subjective.question: Trace the history of the camera from the pinhole camera to the 35mm camera.
subjective.answer: In the 5th century BC, the Chinese philosopher Mozi mentioned the effect of an inverted image forming through a pinhole; Shen Kuo later experimented with a camera obscura and was the first to provide a full geometric and quantitative analysis. The camera obscura was a box with a tiny hole in it, and the structure was perfected in 1558 by Giambattista della Porta. The box camera was reinvented with Kodak's Brownie camera, released in 1900; it cost only $1, was marketed towards children, and became a hit with everyone because of its cheapness and convenience. The first practical 35mm camera was the Leica, built in 1913 by Oskar Barnack; it used standard cinema 35mm film, transported horizontally, with a frame size of 24x36 mm and a 2:3 aspect ratio.

subjective.topic: History of Photography and the Camera
subjective.question: Write a short note on the history of 35mm film.
subjective.answer: 35mm film (more properly, 135 film) is a format of photographic film used for still photography. It is a film with a film gauge of 35mm (1.4 in) loaded into a standardised type of magazine — also referred to as a cassette or cartridge — and used in 135 film cameras. The term 135 was introduced by Kodak in 1934 as a designation for 35mm film specifically for still photography, perforated with Kodak Standard perforations.

subjective.question: What is a rectilinear lens?
subjective.answer: In photography, a rectilinear lens is a photographic lens that yields images where straight features, such as the edges of walls of buildings, appear as straight lines. A rectilinear lens can also be thought of as one that provides little or no distortion.

subjective.question: Describe the main types of camera lenses.
subjective.answer: A prime lens has a fixed focal length; if you want to capture more or less of a subject, you have to physically move closer or farther away, but prime lenses often have better aperture ranges than zoom lenses. A zoom lens has a variable focal length and allows the camera operator to zoom in and out on a subject without moving the camera. A wide-angle lens (about 10 to 42 mm) captures more of a scene and exaggerates the sense of depth. A telephoto lens (about 100 to 800 mm) has a longer focal length, giving a narrower field of view and a compressed sense of depth. A macro lens is a special type of lens used to take close-up pictures of very small subjects at a reproduction ratio of at least 1:1.

subjective.question: Differentiate between a convex lens and a concave lens.
subjective.answer: A convex lens is thicker at the centre than at the edges; it is a converging lens because rays of light that pass through it are brought closer together (they converge), and a convex lens can form a real image. A concave lens is thinner at the centre than at the edges; it is a diverging lens because rays of light that pass through it are spread out (they diverge), and a concave lens can form only a virtual image.

subjective.question: What is a macro lens? What is a microlens?
subjective.answer: A macro lens is a special type of camera lens that has the ability to focus on subjects which are very close to the lens; it can reproduce small items at up to life-size magnification, making it perfect for photographing insects and small products in fine detail. A microlens is a small lens, generally with a diameter of less than a millimetre (mm) and often as small as 10 micrometres (μm); it is generally too small to see with the naked eye.

subjective.question: What is depth of field? How is it related to depth of focus?
subjective.answer: In optics, particularly as it relates to film and photography, depth of field (DOF) is the distance between the closest and the farthest objects in a photo that appear acceptably sharp. It is determined by the distance between the lens and the object, the size of the iris (aperture), and the angle of the lens. Depth of focus describes the relationship between the camera lens and the image plane (film plane or camera sensor) — the distance between the image plane and a focused lens needed to create an in-focus image.

subjective.question: What is exposure in a camera?
subjective.answer: Exposure in a camera is the overall brightness or darkness of a photograph. More precisely, it is the amount of light received by the film or sensor. Exposure is controlled by a combination of shutter speed, film speed, and aperture.

subjective.question: What is film speed (ISO)?
subjective.answer: Film speed is the measure of a photographic film's sensitivity to light, determined by sensitometry and measured on various numerical scales, the most recent being the ISO system. A closely related ISO system is used to describe the relationship between exposure and output image lightness in digital cameras. Relatively insensitive film, with a correspondingly lower speed index, requires more exposure to light to produce the same image density as a more sensitive film, and is thus commonly termed a slow film. Highly sensitive films are correspondingly termed fast films.

subjective.question: What is a light meter?
subjective.answer: A light meter is a device used to measure the amount of light. In photography, an exposure meter (or light meter) is often used to determine the proper exposure for a photograph. The meter will include either a digital or analog calculator which, given the light intensity and either the shutter speed or aperture, calculates the reciprocal value for correct exposure.

subjective.question: Describe the two basic types of light metering.
subjective.answer: There are two basic types of light measurement. With incident measurement, the meter is aimed at the light source. A special translucent cover on the meter collects light from a broad area, simulating the way light falls on a three-dimensional subject; the meter indicates the light level at the subject's position, and the camera exposure is set according to this reading. With reflected measurement, the meter reads the intensity of light reflecting off the subject and indicates an exposure that would render the subject as medium in tone, regardless of its original colours. Meters are designed to regard all subjects as having 18% neutral gray reflectance. The accuracy of a reflected measurement can be improved by reading a gray test card placed in front of the subject.

subjective.question: What is a gray card?
subjective.answer: A gray card is a flat object of neutral colour which can be used as a reference to produce a consistent image exposure and/or colour in film and photography.

subjective.question: What is the Sunny f/16 rule? How does it work?
subjective.answer: The Sunny f/16 rule is a method of estimating correct daylight exposures without a light meter. For daylight on a sunny day, the aperture is set to f/16 and the shutter speed to the inverse of the ISO speed. For example, using ISO 200 film, aperture is set to f/16 and shutter speed to 1/200 second (or as close as possible, e.g. 1/250). The aperture can be changed according to conditions: on a sunny day with distinct shadows, f/16; slightly overcast with soft shadows, f/11; overcast with barely visible shadows, f/8; heavily overcast with no shadows, f/5.6; at sunset, f/4.

subjective.question: What is a UV filter?
subjective.answer: A UV filter is a glass filter that blocks ultraviolet light and is used to prevent haziness and fogging in daylight photographs. UV filters also work to protect the delicate front element of the camera lens. UV filters are very inexpensive, costing just a few dollars each. UV rays, which are invisible to the human eye, can cause a bluish cast in colour photographs and a general lack of sharpness (haziness) in black and white photography.

subjective.question: What is filter factor?
subjective.answer: The amount of exposure compensation needed when a filter is used is often expressed as a filter factor. If the filter factor is 2X, you should multiply the exposure by 2; if it is 4X, multiply the exposure by 4, and so on. Another way to compensate is to divide your ISO by the filter factor: if the filter factor is 2X and your ISO is 200, you should treat your ISO as 100.

subjective.question: What is film grain?
subjective.answer: Film grain or granularity is the random optical texture of processed photographic film due to the presence of small particles of metallic silver, or dye clouds, developed from silver halide that have received enough photons. While film grain is a function of such particles (or dye clouds), it is not the same thing as such: it is an optical effect, the magnitude of which (amount of grain) depends on both the film stock and the definition at which it is observed.

subjective.question: What is the Rule of Thirds?
subjective.answer: The Rule of Thirds, also known as the Rule of Golden Mean, is a composition rule in photography, painting and design. The rule says that an image should be divided into 9 equal parts by 2 vertical and 2 horizontal lines, and that the important elements of a scene should be placed along these lines or at their points of intersection. The rule helps the photographer decide where to place the important compositional elements of a scene.

subjective.question: Differentiate between hard light and soft light.
subjective.answer: Hard light comes from a light source that is relatively small compared to the subject. It casts hard shadows, has a high contrast level, and emphasises textures and details; it is often used in film noir and horror movies and for dramatic portraits. Soft light comes from a light source that is large relative to the subject. It tends to wrap around the subject, filling in shadows and lowering contrast; it is often used in news shows and high-key lighting. Reflectors and diffusers are used to control the light indoors in order to soften and harden it as required.

subjective.question: What is backlighting?
subjective.answer: Backlighting, sometimes referred to as hair light or rim light (although the latter is different), is when the subject is illuminated from the back, facing the viewer.

subjective.question: What is film exposure? How is it controlled?
subjective.answer: Film exposure means exposing photosensitive film to light in a controlled manner in order to record an image. The effect of light on film is proportional to the amount of light; the amount of light is controlled by the intensity of light passing through the lens aperture and by the length of time the film is exposed, which is determined by the shutter speed.

subjective.question: How does a film camera work?
subjective.answer: When a photograph is taken, the shutter opens and light strikes the film inside the camera. This light causes chemical changes in the film emulsion, forming an invisible latent image. Later, in a darkroom, the film is developed in chemical baths which amplify and stabilise the image, and a fixer makes it permanent. For motion pictures, the exposed film travels through the camera: a mechanical claw pulls the film into position behind the shutter, the shutter opens to expose one frame, and the cycle repeats many times per second.

subjective.question: What is a film reel?
subjective.answer: A film reel is a tool originally designed to hold approximately 1,000 feet (300 m) of 35mm motion-picture film and used to wind, unwind, store and transport film in a metal (steel or aluminium) or plastic can.

subjective.question: What are the three stages of production?
subjective.answer: Video production has three stages. The first stage is planning and preparation — pre-production — in which ninety percent of the work on a production goes into planning and preparation. The second stage is the production phase itself, when the recording takes place. The third stage is post-production, which includes editing, additional treatment and duplication of the production.

subjective.question: What are the roles of the producer and the director of photography (DOP)?
subjective.answer: The producer is in charge of the business organisation of the production: generally responsible for the budget, the selection of staff and crew, production scheduling, coordinating the production team, and marketing and distribution of the product. Directors are people who can effectively communicate their vision to the crew. The director of photography (DOP) is the cinematographer, the chief over the camera and lighting crews working on a film, television production or other live-action piece; the DOP is responsible for making artistic and technical decisions related to the image, such as the selection of cameras, film stock, lenses, filters and scene composition.

subjective.question: What is television standards conversion?
subjective.answer: Television standards conversion is the process of changing one type of television system to another; for example, converting a transmission or a recording from one television system (television standard) to another.
